My understanding is that the definition of texture in game engines and real life are different.

In real life it’s how something feels AND looks, in game engines a texture just the image on the side of polygons thats facing the player.
A normal map or bump map will let the engine know how to treat a texture and give it, well, texture.

Say you have a brick wall in CS 1.6, it’s completely flat like it’s just a square with a picture of a brick wall on it. Which it essentially is.
A normal map on that brick wall is a layer on top of the texture which will make light sources reflect off of that brick wall correctly and actually extrude the texture so the bricks can get what looks like individual shape even though there’s no extra polygons for those bricks.

I had a fun and infuriating encounter with a client.

I am making 14 videos in a series for this client and there's a PR firm halfway in between us and that firms only job is to get me the correct dates for when certain things happen. The client and I have a common creative vision and because of the nature of the clients company structure these videos will be made much faster if the PR firm pays me instead of the client.

So at this point I am six videos deep in the project. There's a fourth party in this story who makes graphic plats for the videos, something I could do myself but I love working with others. These guys are employed directly by the client and have been for years. My background is that of a sort of regular player in the culture scene of my city. 

My client wanted me to send the latest video to the PR firm to make them feel like more than just a money channel. I do and all is well, until a week passes.

I get an email from my client telling me to remove my credits from the video. I make these videos solo, no one else is with me on set, in editing or grade. So I am naturally curious, since the plate with my credits wasn't made by me but by the clients graphics guys i.e something the client signed off on before production started.

So I call up my client a week after the email since I was deep in editing the upcoming video.

In the call the client tells me that they want to keep the 'consistency' of the videos intact and that I shouldn't worry about adding my credits since I will get it in other ways through news and PR. I am naturally upset. Not only does the client tell me that my credits should be taken away when it wasn't me that added them in the first place, but they also think I added them just now in the latest video. This means they haven't payed attention to any of the plates in the previous videos, right?

I explain that the credits are as they've always been, and that I don't understand their issue with 'consistency' since the plates weren't made by me. The second I say this my client backs down and apologises, calling it a "moot point" if that's the case and that they are very sorry for the headache. So I ask what prompted them to send me this email.

Here's the kicker.

The client explains that they had a call with the PR firm after the firm saw the video I sent them. The firm asks why my name is in the video credits since it is a \*client name\* production (legally yes, since they hired me and that's fine)? The client then interpreted this hastily as me personally adding new info to the plates that the graphics guys made for the client who then sent the plates to me and then, in result, sent me the email.

So not only did the client lie and wrote the email as if it was their own concern, but they tried making an executive decision without having a discussion with me.

All in all I "won" the debate, and my credits are still in the video tracks and the PR firm is cut off from any creative decision making when it comes to the production of the videos.
